patterns: High-concept optical and neurological glitches: Visualizing how the brain creates illusions, fake vision, or misinterprets reality.
Bizarre physical properties and extreme edge cases: Showing unexpected brain conditions, savants, or unusual physical sensations.
Anthropomorphized brain reactions: Using cute 3D character animation of a brain reacting emotionally to external inputs like food or stress.
Everyday chemical and cognitive hacks: Explaining commonplace experiences like caffeine, learning, or dark psychology tricks using simple analogies.
Active viewer self-testing: Posing interactive challenges where the audience feels their own brain reacting or falling for an illusion in real-time.
title_formulas: Why Your Brain Can't [Counterintuitive Physical Action] [Emoji]
This Is What Happens To Your Brain When You [Common Daily Action] [Emoji]
How Your Brain Hacks [Perceptual Phenomenon or Sensation]
opening_3s: A striking 3D visual of a brain reacting instantly to a jarring stimulus accompanied by a direct question.
A bizarre physical mystery demonstrated immediately on screen before explaining the underlying neural cause.
An interactive visual prompt asking the viewer to stare at a specific point to trigger an immediate cognitive sensation.
comment_themes: Relatable self-testing comments where viewers confirm feeling the exact mental effect described in the video.
Affection for charming visual metaphors, especially cute or personified representations of organs.
Dark humor and pop-culture references sparked by unusual medical facts or mind-control concepts.
Requests for explanations of everyday physical phenomena like post-meal sleepiness or sensory oddities.
avoid: Overly clinical medical explanations without clear, relatable visual metaphors.
Audio tracks or music that clash with the visual tone and make informative content feel unnerving.
Generic tip listicles that lack an immediate visual demonstration or high-stakes hook.
try_next: A 35-second breakdown of phantom limb sensations using historical cases from classic neurology texts with stylized 3D visualization.
A 28-second interactive video demonstrating how auditory visual illusions trick perception, asking viewers to test it with headphones.
A 40-second animated story of a historical psychological experiment illustrating how muscle memory forms while sleeping.
